title: Walnut Burfi: A Rich, Nutty Indian Sweet That Comes Together in 25 Minutes
excerpt: Also known as akhrot barfi, this fudgy mithai uses just four main ingredients and makes an elegant homemade gift for any festival.
body:
• Walnut burfi (akhrot barfi) is a traditional Indian fudge made with ground walnuts, sugar, ghee, and cardamom — just four core ingredients
  • The recipe takes about 25 minutes of active cooking plus cooling time, and is forgiving enough for beginners
  • Roasting walnuts on low heat is the critical step — high heat scorches the oils and turns the burfi bitter
  • The sweet stores for up to a week at room temperature in an airtight container and up to two weeks when refrigerated

Walnut burfi — also called akhrot barfi — belongs to the same family of Indian milk fudges as kaju katli and besan barfi, but gets its richness from walnuts rather than cashews or chickpea flour. The result is a denser, earthier sweet with a fudgy bite that pairs beautifully with cardamom.

The sweet is popular across North India, particularly in Kashmiri and Punjabi households where walnuts grow in abundance. It is a festive staple during Diwali, Navratri, and Raksha Bandhan, and works just as well as an everyday treat or a homemade gift.

Ingredients

"Low heat is critical — walnuts burn quickly and turn bitter."

  • 1 cup walnuts (akhrot), shelled
  • 1 cup sugar
  • ¼ cup ghee
  • ½ teaspoon cardamom powder (elaichi)
  • ¼ cup water
  • Chopped pistachios and almonds, for garnish
  • A little ghee, for greasing the tray

Step-by-Step Recipe

  1. Roast the walnuts. Heat a dry pan on low flame. Add the walnuts and roast for 3–4 minutes, stirring constantly, until they turn lightly golden and fragrant. Low heat is critical — walnuts burn quickly and turn bitter.
  2. Grind to a coarse powder. Let the roasted walnuts cool for a few minutes. Transfer them to a blender or mixer grinder and pulse to a coarse powder. Do not over-grind into a paste — some texture in the burfi is what gives it character.
  3. Make the sugar syrup. In a heavy-bottomed pan, combine the sugar with ¼ cup of water. Stir over medium heat until the sugar dissolves completely. Continue cooking until the syrup reaches one-string consistency — when you press a drop between your thumb and forefinger and pull apart, a single thread should form.
  4. Combine. Add the ground walnut powder and ghee to the sugar syrup. Stir continuously on medium-low heat for 5–7 minutes until the mixture thickens and begins to leave the sides of the pan.
  5. Add cardamom. Sprinkle in the cardamom powder and mix well.
  6. Set the burfi. Grease a plate or tray with ghee. Pour the walnut mixture onto it and spread evenly using a spatula. Garnish with chopped pistachios and almonds, pressing them gently into the surface.
  7. Cool and cut. Let the burfi cool to room temperature for 30–45 minutes. Once firm, cut into diamond or square shapes with a sharp knife.

Tips for the Perfect Batch

  • Roast on low heat. High heat scorches the walnut oils, leaving a bitter aftertaste. Patience here makes the difference between good and great burfi.
  • Test the sugar syrup. One-string consistency is essential. Too thin, and the burfi will not set. Too thick, and it becomes hard and crystallized.
  • Use fresh walnuts. Stale walnuts taste rancid. Kashmiri or Californian walnuts both work well.
  • Add saffron for colour. A pinch of saffron dissolved in a tablespoon of warm milk gives the burfi a golden hue and a subtle fragrance.
  • Mawa variation. For an even richer version, replace half the sugar syrup with crumbled mawa (khoya). Sauté the mawa first until it releases its fat, then fold in the walnut powder and sugar, according to chef Sanjeev Kapoor's recipe.

Why Walnuts Deserve a Spot in Your Mithai Rotation

Walnuts are among the most nutrient-dense nuts available. A quarter cup provides about 4.5 grams of protein and 2.5 grams of plant-based omega-3 fatty acids, along with generous amounts of manganese and copper. In Ayurveda, they are classified as brain-nourishing foods — a tradition reinforced by modern research linking walnut consumption to improved cognitive function.

For NRI families, walnut burfi is an easy way to introduce kids to homemade Indian sweets without the hours that more elaborate mithai demand. The recipe is forgiving enough for beginners and impressive enough to bring to a dinner party or pack into a Diwali gift box.
